entries.meaning: A large metal basket on wheels that you push around a store. ---
examples: Grab a shopping cart on your way in.
All the shopping carts were still out in the parking lot.
My shopping cart had a wheel that kept sticking.

entries.meaning: A written list of the things you plan to buy. ---
examples: Don't go to the store without a shopping list.
Our shopping lists are always longer than our budget.
Milk is at the top of the shopping list.

entries.meaning: A large building holding many stores under one roof. ---
examples: The kids want to hang out at the shopping mall.
Two shopping malls in this town have closed down.
There's a movie theater inside the shopping mall.

entries.meaning: A group of stores built together with a shared parking lot. ---
examples: There's a new shopping center out by the highway.
Both shopping centers have a pharmacy.
The bank is in the same shopping center as the bakery.
entries.contrast: American spelling. British English writes 'shopping centre'.

entries.meaning: The line of customers waiting to pay in a store. ---
examples: The checkout line wrapped around the display of soda.
Pick the shortest of the checkout lines.
I always end up in the slowest checkout line.
entries.contrast: Americans stand in a 'line'; the British stand in a 'queue'.

entries.meaning: The surface where you put your items to be scanned and paid for. ---
examples: He emptied the basket onto the checkout counter.
Candy is stacked by every checkout counter.
I left my keys on the checkout counter.

entries.meaning: A machine that lets a customer scan and pay for items without a cashier. ---
examples: I used the self-checkout to save time.
Three of the self-checkouts were out of order.
The self-checkout kept telling me to remove the item from the bagging area.

entries.meaning: The small label on an item showing what it costs. ---
examples: I checked the price tag and put the jacket back.
Someone had switched the price tags on two of the lamps.
The price tag was still hanging off the sleeve.

entries.meaning: One single thing among the things being bought or sold. ---
examples: That lane is for ten items or fewer.
Each item is rung up separately.
The last item on my list was coffee.

entries.meaning: The act of trading a bought item for a different one. ---
examples: They gave me an even exchange for a larger size.
The store allows exchanges within thirty days.
Without the tag, no refund and no exchange.

entries.meaning: A store's rules about bringing merchandise back. ---
examples: Read the return policy before you buy the mattress.
Their return policies changed after the holidays.
The return policy is printed on the back of the receipt.

entries.meaning: A card loaded with money that can be spent at a particular store. ---
examples: My aunt sends a gift card every birthday.
I still have two gift cards in my wallet from last year.
The gift card had eleven dollars left on it.

entries.meaning: A printed document worth a set amount at a store or restaurant. ---
examples: They won a fifty-dollar gift certificate to the steakhouse.
The salon sells gift certificates at the front desk.
The gift certificate expires at the end of the year.

entries.meaning: A bank card that takes money straight out of your account when you pay. ---
examples: I paid with my debit card instead of cash.
Some vending machines take debit cards now.
My debit card was declined at the register.

entries.meaning: The tax added to the price of goods at the moment you buy them. ---
examples: The sticker says nine dollars, but sales tax brings it to nine sixty.
Oregon doesn't charge sales tax.
Groceries are exempt from sales tax in this state.

entries.meaning: A short code typed in online to get a discount. ---
examples: Enter the promo code at checkout.
None of the promo codes I found actually worked.
The promo code took fifteen percent off.

entries.meaning: The lower price an item is sold for during a sale. ---
examples: The sale price is good through Sunday.
Sale prices are marked in red.
They rang it up at the regular price instead of the sale price.

entries.meaning: The official published price of something before any discount. ---
examples: Nobody pays the list price for a car.
List prices went up again this spring.
We got it for six hundred under list price.

entries.meaning: The price an ordinary customer pays in a store. ---
examples: The retail price is nearly double what it costs to make.
Retail prices on electronics keep falling.
Employees pay half the retail price.

entries.meaning: The span between the lowest and highest price you will consider or find. ---
examples: Those couches are out of my price range.
They carry bikes in three different price ranges.
Tell me your price range and I'll show you some options.

entries.meaning: The cost of one ounce, pound or piece, used to compare packages. ---
examples: Check the unit price on the shelf label.
The unit prices are printed in small type.
The big box has a lower unit price than the small one.

entries.meaning: The price shown on the label, before fees or bargaining. ---
examples: The sticker price doesn't include tax.
Sticker prices on new trucks shocked us.
He talked the dealer down from the sticker price.

entries.meaning: A slip letting you buy a sold-out sale item later at the sale price. ---
examples: They gave me a rain check for the chicken.
The manager writes rain checks at the service desk.
My rain check is good for thirty days.
entries.русский: талон на покупку по акции позже

entries.meaning: A request for a clerk to confirm what an item costs. ---
examples: The cashier called for a price check on the melons.
Two price checks held up the whole line.
Can I get a price check on this jacket?

entries.meaning: A store's agreement to sell at a competitor's lower price. ---
examples: I asked for a price match and showed them the ad.
They don't do price matches on clearance items.
The price match saved me thirty bucks.
entries.русский: продажа по цене конкурента, выравнивание цены

entries.meaning: A plan where a store holds an item until the customer has paid for it. ---
examples: She put the bike on layaway in October.
The store brought back layaway for the holidays.
You lose the deposit if you cancel the layaway.

entries.meaning: An arrangement to pay for something over time instead of all at once. ---
examples: The furniture store offers financing with no interest for a year.
We qualified for financing on the washer and dryer.
Read the fine print before you accept the financing.

entries.meaning: An agreement to pay in equal amounts over several months. ---
examples: We bought the mattress on an installment plan.
Their installment plans run six or twelve months.
The installment plan costs four hundred a month.
entries.contrast: American spells it with two l's; British English writes 'instalment'.

entries.meaning: Money a store gives back that can only be spent in that store. ---
examples: Without a receipt you only get store credit.
I have forty dollars in store credit left.
They refused cash and offered store credit instead.

entries.meaning: Cash handed to you at the register on top of your purchase, or money returned on card spending. ---
examples: Do you want any cash back with that?
I took twenty dollars in cash back at the grocery store.
The card gives two percent cash back on gas.

entries.meaning: The help a store gives its shoppers before and after they buy. ---
examples: The customer service at that store is terrible.
Take it to the customer service desk in the back.
I spent an hour on hold with customer service.

entries.meaning: A written opinion a buyer posts about a product or store. ---
examples: I read every customer review before ordering.
The customer reviews warned that it runs small.
One angry customer review mentioned a broken zipper.

entries.meaning: Something expensive and pleasant that you do not really need. ---
examples: A second car is a luxury we can't afford.
We cut out small luxuries like takeout coffee.
For her, a long bath is a real luxury.

entries.meaning: Something you genuinely need rather than simply want. ---
examples: A phone is a necessity now, not a treat.
We only bought necessities that month.
Bread and milk are the sort of necessity the corner store sells.

entries.meaning: A shopper who looks hard for the lowest prices. ---
examples: My mother is a serious bargain hunter.
Bargain hunters lined up before the doors opened.
As a bargain hunter, he never pays full price.

entries.meaning: Something bought suddenly without planning to. ---
examples: The sunglasses were a total impulse buy.
Candy by the register is designed for impulse buys.
That jacket was an impulse buy I regretted by Monday.

entries.meaning: Looking at goods in stores without intending to buy. ---
examples: We did some window shopping downtown.
Window shopping is free entertainment.
A little window shopping killed the hour before the movie.

entries.meaning: A burst of buying a lot of things at once. ---
examples: She went on a shopping spree after her bonus came through.
Their shopping sprees always end at the shoe store.
One shopping spree wiped out my savings.
entries.русский: поход по магазинам с крупными тратами

entries.meaning: One outing made in order to buy things. ---
examples: We make one big shopping trip a month.
Two shopping trips and I still forgot the batteries.
The shopping trip took all afternoon.

entries.meaning: A short trip to buy something or do a small task. ---
examples: I have one more errand before dinner.
She ran errands all Saturday morning.
Picking up the dry cleaning is a quick errand.
entries.русский: поручение, дело (сходить в магазин и т.п.)

entries.meaning: A list of food and household items to buy. ---
examples: Add eggs to the grocery list.
We keep our grocery lists on the refrigerator.
He shops straight down the grocery list.

entries.meaning: A very large store selling a huge range of goods. ---
examples: The superstore out on the highway sells everything.
Two superstores opened the same year.
You can get tires and groceries at the same superstore.

entries.meaning: A huge plain warehouse-style chain store on the edge of town. ---
examples: A big-box store moved in and the hardware shop closed.
Big-box stores ring the whole suburb.
The big-box store has its own gas station.

entries.meaning: A members-only store selling goods in very large packages. ---
examples: We buy paper towels at the warehouse club.
Both warehouse clubs charge an annual membership.
The warehouse club sells rotisserie chickens for five dollars.

entries.meaning: One of many stores of the same company under the same name. ---
examples: The chain store undercut every local shop.
Chain stores took over the whole downtown.
Every chain store has the exact same layout.

entries.meaning: A small neighborhood shop selling everyday items. ---
examples: Run to the corner store for milk.
The corner stores stay open when the supermarket closes.
The corner store cashes checks for regulars.
entries.contrast: American. The British equivalent is a 'corner shop'.

entries.meaning: A store that sells alcoholic drinks to take home. ---
examples: The liquor store closes at nine on Sundays.
Liquor stores are state-run in some places.
He stopped at the liquor store for a bottle of wine.
entries.contrast: 'Liquor' is LIK-ur; the qu sounds like plain k. Britain has an 'off-licence'.

entries.meaning: A store selling used clothes and household goods cheaply, often for charity. ---
examples: She found a leather jacket at the thrift store for six dollars.
We hit three thrift stores in one afternoon.
The thrift store takes donations at the side door.

entries.meaning: A store that sells other people's used goods and splits the money with them. ---
examples: She sells her old dresses at a consignment shop.
The consignment shops on that street take only designer labels.
The consignment shop keeps forty percent of the sale.
entries.contrast: The g in 'consignment' is silent: kun-SYNE-munt.

entries.meaning: A store where most items cost a dollar or two. ---
examples: I get wrapping paper at the dollar store.
There are four dollar stores within a mile of here.
The dollar store had exactly what I needed for the party.

entries.meaning: A shopping center where brands sell their goods at reduced prices. ---
examples: The outlet mall is an hour up the interstate.
Outlet malls are packed the week after Christmas.
We bought her school clothes at the outlet mall.

entries.meaning: A store selling animals and supplies for them. ---
examples: The kids beg to visit the pet store every week.
Most pet stores here no longer sell puppies.
I get birdseed at the pet store down the block.
entries.contrast: American pet store; the British say pet shop.

entries.meaning: A store that sells toys and games for children. ---
examples: The toy store was mobbed in December.
Old-fashioned toy stores are getting rare.
He spent his birthday money at the toy store.

entries.meaning: A store that sells footwear. ---
examples: The shoe store measured both of my feet.
There are two shoe stores at the mall.
That shoe store carries wide sizes.

entries.meaning: A store that sells clothes. ---
examples: She manages a clothing store at the mall.
The clothing stores start their sales in July.
This clothing store has a great sale rack.

entries.meaning: A store selling rings, necklaces and watches. ---
examples: He bought the ring at a jewelry store downtown.
The jewelry stores keep everything in locked cases.
The jewelry store cleans your rings for free.
entries.contrast: American 'jewelry' has two syllables; British 'jewellery' has three.

entries.meaning: A small store selling presents and souvenirs. ---
examples: The museum gift shop sells postcards and mugs.
Hospital gift shops always have flowers.
We got out through the gift shop, of course.

entries.meaning: A sale of unwanted household things held at someone's home. ---
examples: We're having a garage sale on Saturday.
He drives around to garage sales looking for tools.
I bought this lamp for two dollars at a garage sale.
entries.contrast: Americans stress 'garage' on the second syllable: guh-RAHZH.

entries.meaning: A sale of used belongings spread out in front of a house. ---
examples: There's a yard sale two streets over.
Half the block held yard sales the same morning.
The yard sale signs are stapled to every telephone pole.

entries.meaning: A sale of the entire contents of a house, usually after a death or a move. ---
examples: They found the china cabinet at an estate sale.
Estate sales are listed in the Thursday paper.
The estate sale started at eight and everything good was gone by nine.
entries.русский: распродажа имущества (после переезда или смерти владельца)

entries.meaning: An open-air market where people sell used and cheap goods from tables. ---
examples: The swap meet fills the drive-in lot every Sunday.
You can haggle at swap meets.
He sells car parts at the swap meet.

entries.meaning: A large room where goods such as cars or furniture are displayed for sale. ---
examples: The new models are in the showroom out front.
Their showrooms are open until eight.
We walked around the showroom for an hour without buying anything.

entries.meaning: The back room of a store where extra goods are kept. ---
examples: Let me check the stockroom for a size ten.
The stockrooms are packed before the holidays.
He spent his first month unloading boxes in the stockroom.

entries.meaning: The part of a store where goods are displayed and customers walk around. ---
examples: She works the sales floor on weekends.
The sales floors were rearranged overnight.
Nobody was on the sales floor to answer questions.

entries.meaning: A small room in a store where you try clothes on. ---
examples: The fitting room is behind the shoe display.
All the fitting rooms were taken.
You can bring six items into the fitting room.

entries.meaning: Dressing room has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She left the jeans in the dressing room.
The dressing rooms are down the hall on the left.
There's a mirror inside the dressing room.
Flowers were waiting in her dressing room.
The dressing rooms are down the hall past the green room.
Four of us shared one tiny dressing room.

senses.head: A private space in a store for trying on clothing
examples: She left the jeans in the dressing room.
The dressing rooms are down the hall on the left.
There's a mirror inside the dressing room.

senses.head: A room backstage where performers change and put on makeup
examples: Flowers were waiting in her dressing room.
The dressing rooms are down the hall past the green room.
Four of us shared one tiny dressing room.

entries.meaning: The rack holding marked-down items a store wants to get rid of. ---
examples: Everything on the clearance rack is under ten dollars.
I always check the clearance racks first.
She found the dress on a clearance rack in the back.

entries.meaning: A checkout for shoppers buying only a few items. ---
examples: Take the express lane if you only have milk.
Both express lanes were closed.
The man ahead of me had thirty items in the express lane.
entries.русский: касса для покупателей с несколькими товарами

entries.meaning: A store worker who serves customers and rings up sales. ---
examples: The salesclerk wrapped the vase in tissue.
Two salesclerks were folding sweaters.
I asked the salesclerk where the batteries were.
entries.contrast: Americans say KLURK; the British say 'clerk' as KLARK.

entries.meaning: The usual American job title for a store employee who helps shoppers. ---
examples: He was hired as a sales associate at the electronics store.
The sales associates wear red vests.
Ask any sales associate to open the case for you.

entries.meaning: A person who visits businesses to sell a company's products. ---
examples: The sales rep comes by every other Tuesday.
Their sales reps cover three states.
A sales rep left samples with the store manager.

entries.meaning: A grocery store worker who puts purchases into bags. ---
examples: The bagger asked if I wanted paper or plastic.
The baggers also collect carts from the lot.
He worked as a bagger the summer after high school.

entries.meaning: A person who owns or runs a small store. ---
examples: The shopkeeper knows every customer by name.
Local shopkeepers signed a petition about the parking.
The shopkeeper locked up and pulled down the shade.

entries.meaning: The person or business offering something for sale. ---
examples: The seller shipped it the same day.
Some sellers on that site have no reviews.
I messaged the seller about the scratch on the lens.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'cellar', the room under a house.

entries.meaning: A person who steals goods from a store. ---
examples: A shoplifter set off the alarm at the door.
The sign warns that shoplifters will be prosecuted.
Security caught the shoplifter in the parking lot.

entries.meaning: The code that lets you follow a package on its way to you. ---
examples: They emailed me a tracking number.
Both tracking numbers show the same delivery date.
The tracking number hasn't updated in three days.

entries.meaning: The system of buying goods that are sent to you by mail. ---
examples: Her grandmother bought everything by mail order.
The company started as a mail order seed business.
Mail order was the internet shopping of its day.

entries.meaning: A website where a business sells its goods. ---
examples: Their online store has more colors than the shop does.
Small online stores often ship slower.
The online store was down all morning.

entries.meaning: The business of buying and selling over the internet. ---
examples: E-commerce took a huge bite out of mall traffic.
She works in e-commerce for a clothing brand.
Their whole e-commerce operation runs from one warehouse.

entries.meaning: A saved list of things you would like to buy or be given. ---
examples: I put the headphones on my wish list.
The kids emailed their wish lists to grandma.
Half the things on my wish list went on sale.

entries.meaning: A store plan that rewards regular customers with points or discounts. ---
examples: Their loyalty program gives you a free coffee every tenth visit.
I've signed up for too many loyalty programs.
The loyalty program takes your email address.

entries.meaning: A card that records your purchases so you earn discounts. ---
examples: Scan your loyalty card before you pay.
My keychain is buried in loyalty cards.
The sale price only applies with a loyalty card.

entries.meaning: The amount paid to belong to a club store or program. ---
examples: The membership fee is sixty dollars a year.
They raised their membership fees in January.
You save more than the membership fee in one trip.

entries.meaning: A receipt without the price, so the person can exchange the gift. ---
examples: Can I get a gift receipt with that?
She tucks gift receipts into the card.
Without a gift receipt he was stuck with the sweater.
entries.contrast: The p in 'receipt' is silent: rih-SEET.

entries.meaning: A sturdy bag a shopper brings back to the store each time. ---
examples: I left the reusable bags in the car again.
Bring a reusable bag or you'll pay for one.
The store gives out a free reusable bag on Earth Day.

entries.meaning: A small hand basket for carrying a few items around a store. ---
examples: Take a shopping basket instead of a cart.
The shopping baskets are stacked by the entrance.
My shopping basket got heavy fast.

entries.meaning: The range of goods a store offers to choose from. ---
examples: That store has a great selection of cheese.
Their online selections are bigger than in the shop.
The selection thins out by Sunday night.

entries.meaning: Variety has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The market carries a wide variety of apples.
They stock a dozen varieties of hot sauce.
There's not much variety at the corner store.
That variety ripens two weeks earlier.
The nursery carries about ten varieties of apple.
Ask for a variety that does well in heat.

senses.head: A number of different kinds of something available
examples: The market carries a wide variety of apples.
They stock a dozen varieties of hot sauce.
There's not much variety at the corner store.

senses.head: A named kind of plant within a species
examples: That variety ripens two weeks earlier.
The nursery carries about ten varieties of apple.
Ask for a variety that does well in heat.

entries.meaning: An order for goods the seller does not have in stock yet. ---
examples: The chair is on backorder until March.
They have hundreds of backorders to fill.
My backorder finally shipped six weeks late.

entries.meaning: A final sale of the last of a line of goods at low prices. ---
examples: The tile was a closeout, so there's no matching more.
They buy closeouts from big chains and resell them.
Everything in that aisle is a closeout.

entries.meaning: An old item given to a seller as part of the payment for a new one. ---
examples: They gave me two hundred dollars for the trade-in.
The store accepts trade-ins on old phones.
My car was worth more as a trade-in than I expected.
entries.русский: сдача старой вещи в счёт новой

entries.meaning: A cheap copy of a well-known branded product. ---
examples: That handbag is an obvious knockoff.
The stalls were full of knockoffs.
For twenty dollars you're buying a knockoff.
entries.contrast: The k in 'knock' is silent: NAHK-awf.

entries.meaning: A fake item made to pass as the genuine article. ---
examples: The watch turned out to be a counterfeit.
Customs seized a truckload of counterfeits.
It's hard to spot a good counterfeit.

entries.meaning: A copy of something better or more expensive. ---
examples: The frame is an imitation of an antique.
Cheap imitations showed up within a month.
It's an imitation, but it looks convincing.

entries.meaning: A cheaper product sold under the store's own name. ---
examples: The store brand cereal tastes the same to me.
Store brands are usually a third cheaper.
I buy the store brand for everything but coffee.

entries.meaning: The name a manufacturer gives its product line. ---
examples: People pay extra for the brand name.
Half these brand names belong to the same company.
The pills are identical except for the brand name.

entries.meaning: A name or symbol legally registered to one company. ---
examples: The name is a registered trademark.
They own trademarks in a dozen countries.
Using that trademark got the shop a letter from a lawyer.

entries.meaning: The date printed on a product after which it should not be used. ---
examples: Check the expiration date on the milk.
The expiration dates are stamped on the bottom.
This yogurt is a week past its expiration date.

entries.meaning: The length of time a product stays good on the shelf. ---
examples: Canned soup has a long shelf life.
The two brands have very different shelf lives.
Fresh bread has a shelf life of about three days.

entries.meaning: Something sold at an unfairly high price. ---
examples: Nine dollars for a bottle of water is a rip-off.
Airport shops are famous rip-offs.
The extended warranty is a total rip-off.

entries.meaning: Something a store gives you at no cost. ---
examples: The tote bag was a freebie with the purchase.
She collects freebies from every conference.
They threw in a freebie because of the delay.

entries.meaning: An event where a store hands out free items or prizes. ---
examples: The store is holding a giveaway on opening day.
Their giveaways always draw a crowd.
I entered the giveaway for a free grill.

entries.meaning: A device attached to merchandise that sets off an alarm if it leaves the store. ---
examples: The cashier forgot to take off the security tag.
Security tags are on every leather jacket.
I had to drive back to have the security tag removed.

entries.meaning: An extra charge added on top of the normal price. ---
examples: There's a small surcharge for paying by card.
Fuel surcharges raised every delivery price.
The surcharge wasn't mentioned until the register.

entries.meaning: The small machine you tap, insert or swipe a payment card on. ---
examples: Insert your chip into the card reader.
Both card readers are down, so it's cash only.
The card reader asked if I wanted to leave a tip.

entries.meaning: The arrangement of goods in a store window to attract shoppers. ---
examples: The window display is all red for Valentine's Day.
Their holiday window displays draw crowds every December.
A mannequin fell over in the window display.

entries.meaning: Shopping done to cheer yourself up. ---
examples: After the breakup she went in for some retail therapy.
A little retail therapy never hurt anybody.
He calls it retail therapy; his wife calls it a problem.

entries.meaning: A sharp increase in what something costs.
examples: Customers complained about the price hike on eggs.
Two price hikes in one year drove people away.
The price hike took effect on the first of the month.
